title: Exploding the Notion of “Preludes and Fugues in Various Keys” in Expanded Universe
content_blocks: When I tell non-musician friends I’ve released recordings of preludes and fugues for piano, many of them ask “what is a fugue?” They could also ask “what is a prelude?” and “what is a key?”, since Expanded Universe explodes those very notions.

So what is a ‘key’? It’s a group of notes—sometimes called a scale—which begins and ends with one particular note (the tonic or keynote). ‘C major’ refers to the notes in the C-major scale, with C as the tonic, and the other notes relating to it in particular ways. ‘Scale’ can be misleading, though: derived from the Latin word for ladder, it suggests that melodies must go up or down that ladder, one step at a time. But melodies often make jumps or leaps over any number of steps of the ladder, or mix leaps and steps.

A better term is ‘mode’: a collection of characteristic melodies found in music in that mode, with a particular tonic. A mode emerges from and exerts an influence on actual music—it is not pre-existing, but evolves with and shapes music over time. ‘Mode’ is also useful in broadening our idea of what western classical music can be about. For there really are only two ‘keys’—major and minor (with twelve different possible tonics, yielding 24 major and minor keys)—but there are hundreds if not thousands of modes in world cultures.

The thirteen prelude-and-fugues in Expanded Universe are written in a total of seven different modes, all but one of which were newly devised for this set. But wait: if the definition of ‘mode’ refers to a collection of characteristic melodies found in the music in that mode, how can a mode be newly created? Well, these new modes are unexplored universes, inviting the creation of new characteristic melodies.

Now to ‘fugue’. In a traditional fugue, a short melody (the subject) is presented in one particular range—high, medium, or low—called a ‘voice’. After it reaches a brief resting point, the same or nearly the same melody will be presented in a higher or lower range, beginning on a different, related note. Meanwhile, the first voice will continue with different material that goes with the original melody. This continues until all of the voices in the piece have entered, leading to a moment of rest in all of the voices. Later sections may work similarly, or the second voice may no longer “politely” (a term that my colleague Ian Krouse uses) wait for the first voice to finish—the distance between the start of one voice and the start of the next may narrow (termed a stretto in Italian). Other transformations of the subject are also possible: it may be stretched out, compressed, turned upside down, or transformed in other, less expected ways.

The notion of ‘Fugue’ in Expanded Universe is exploded first with respect to mode, as the traditional ideas of resting point and of related notes are tied to major or minor modes. But the pieces also explore different ways for a fugue to unfold, including the rhythms, textures, ranges, characteristics, and other changes that happen over the course of the piece.

Lastly, the idea of ‘prelude’—establishing the key and mood of the prelude-and-fugue pair—is also exploded.  Some blur the line between prelude and fugue; one uses a fugue to fulfill the function of the prelude (and then uses prelude-like music for the fugue); and some explore distinctly different melodies in the newly-created modes from what the fugue employs.

On the whole Expanded Universe pushes the outside of the envelope of what a prelude and fugue can or should be. These are modal preludes and fugues, in which our tolerances for breaking rules are pushed to the limits.
